ety.text: According to Kulakovskiĭ, from Evenki екэ (jekə), but the Russian word was probably corrupted from the form of another Tungusic language. Most likely ultimately from Proto-Turkic *yaka (“collar; edge”), referring to the location of the Yakut (Sakha) people in Siberia, and therefore a doublet of саха́ (saxá), from Yakut саха (saqa), from the Proto-Turkic via the sound change *ǰaqa → *čaqa. Compare Turkish yaka (“collar, edge, border”). The ending -ут (-ut) possibly contains the Mongolic plural suffix; compare Buryat яхад (jaxad, “Yakuts”).
